text: The scan connexion appears to misidentify the strategic interface. P does not elicit reports from embodied agents: at each step an external LMM compares egocentric observations via \(M_{ij}=f_{\mathrm{LMM}}(o_i,o_j,\Theta)\) (P, Method, LMM Pairwise Comparison), while Q’s revelation principle concerns a privately informed agent choosing a report and then an action, and IC must deter joint misreport/disobedience deviations (Q, around lines 372–396). Bradley–Terry consistency only recovers a fixed latent comparator vector under its model; it does not imply truthful behavior or robustness to endogenous observation manipulation. Thus Q cannot directly provide an IC proof for P as written.

I will pursue a sharper connection: MARS-RA makes comparison-visible behavior an endogenous reward target, so trained agents may manipulate what the LMM sees. I will test whether P’s potential-shaping construction neutralizes this incentive or instead supplies a concrete mechanism-design vulnerability, and whether Q’s obedience/double-deviation framework yields a defensible audit or redesign.

I will test the abstract-level proposed connection against the actual information flow in P, then focus on the narrower question whether MARS-RA's observation-to-credit channel creates strategically manipulable evidence and whether Q's incentive-compatibility machinery applies.

The proposed connection is not valid as stated. P, lines around its LMM comparison subsection, defines \((M_t)_{i,j}=f_{\mathrm{LMM}}(o_t^i,o_t^j,\Theta)\): an external LMM receives agents' egocentric images; the agents submit no capability/contribution reports. P's robustness proposition only proves concentration of Bradley--Terry MLE around the LMM's stable latent preference \(c_t^*\), at rate \(O(\sqrt{n\log n/K})\); it neither identifies \(c_t^*\) with true contribution nor handles endogenous/strategic corruption. Indeed its Shapley proposition explicitly assumes \(c_t^*=v_t^*\). Thus rank aggregation filters sampling noise but cannot by itself supply incentive compatibility.

Sharper joint question: can a policy strategically alter its observable trajectory to win MARS-RA comparisons without improving team return, and can an incentive-compatible peer-evidence layer prevent such credit gaming? Q supplies the distinction between honesty and obedience and a peer-scoring sufficient condition: distinct types must induce distinct beliefs over co-player reports, \(\beta_i[t_i]\neq\beta_i[\hat t_i]\), with truthful-score gap \(\Lambda\|\beta_i[t_i]-\beta_i[\hat t_i]\|_2^2\). P supplies a concrete embodied MARL testbed and an observation-based reward channel. This is more specific than generic strategic misreporting because MARS-RA makes perceived relative contribution itself a learned, policy-relevant potential.

The abstract-level connexion conflates statistical robustness with incentive robustness. P never solicits agent reports: an external LMM compares fixed egocentric images, assumes a stable Bradley--Terry latent vector, and proves concentration around that vector. Q's incentive compatibility instead concerns strategic agents choosing reports and actions under report/action-contingent rewards. Thus rank aggregation alone cannot imply robustness to strategic misreporting; the relevant strategic channel in P is agents changing actions or observations to game the LMM evaluator, not corrupting comparison entries directly.

A key limitation of the credit-gaming idea is P\x27s PBRS algebra. With the same discount factor and terminal potential zero, each agent\x27s discounted shaping return telescopes: \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t[\gamma\psi_i(s_{t+1},t+1)-\psi_i(s_t,t)]=-\psi_i(s_0,0)+\gamma^T\psi_i(s_T,T)=-\psi_i(s_0,0)\). For fixed initial state this gives no policy-level gain from merely making later observations look contributive. Therefore a claim that MARS-RA creates a new strategic optimum is false under its stated ideal conditions. Any vulnerability must be located in violations of the telescoping setup (recomputed/inconsistent boundary potentials, discount mismatch, truncation/nonzero terminal potential), learning dynamics/function approximation, or an external payoff tied directly to reported credit. Q does not analyze these MARL approximation effects.

The observation-gaming proposal needs a major qualification. P defines per-agent shaping \(F_{i,t}=\gamma\psi_i(s_{t+1},t+1)-\psi_i(s_t,t)\), with terminal potential zero. If agents optimize the same \(\gamma\)-discounted full-episode return and \(\psi_i\) is well-defined on every augmented state, then pathwise \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^tF_{i,t}=-\psi_i(s_0,0)+\gamma^T\psi_i(s_T,T)=-\psi_i(s_0,0)\). Intermediate attempts to win comparisons cannot improve return. This is exactly why P claims policy/Nash invariance. Strategic effects can arise only through a broken premise: truncated/approximate learning updates, policy-dependent initial potential, or ill-defined lifecycle boundaries when active-set softmax credits appear/disappear. Any proposed gaming experiment must isolate one of these, not merely adversarial behavior.

A pair-specific publication line is therefore an incentive-boundary audit for open-team PBRS: characterize when MARS-RA’s active-coalition, vector potential remains a genuine potential and when agent exit/re-entry or rollout truncation creates uncompensated boundary payments. P defines \(\hat c_t\in\mathbb R^{|I^t|}\), softmaxes over the active coalition, skips comparisons for \(|I^t|<2\), and temporarily removes/respawns depleted agents; it does not specify how \(\psi_i\) is continued across dimension changes. Q supplies the correct audit criterion: block action deviations jointly with any feasible concealment/report deviation, rather than infer incentives from estimator consistency. A theorem can show invariance/IC under a globally defined augmented-state potential with explicit entry/exit settlement, and a counterexample otherwise; MARS-Bench can test policies that time battery depletion, re-entry, or evaluator visibility around boundaries.

A sharper pair-specific issue is P's open-team boundary. P defines \(\psi(s_t,t)=\operatorname{softmax}(\hat{\boldsymbol c}_t)\) only over active agents, so its dimension is \(|I^t|\), yet writes \(F_t=\gamma\psi_{t+1}-\psi_t\) across transitions where \(I^{t+1}\neq I^t\). This is not defined without an identity-preserving embedding. If scores are padded into a fixed population and every entry/exit transition remains in each agent's accounted return, shaping telescopes to an action-independent endpoint term. If an agent's return is truncated at removal, a boundary term remains and action-dependent battery depletion can make exit timing strategically valuable. Q's honesty-plus-obedience lens then applies specifically to participation/capability concealment, unlike the proposed generic misreport story.

Publication line: participation-safe rank-based reward shaping in open MARL. First formalize fixed identities and an inactive state, then prove a dichotomy: full-episode fixed-dimensional PBRS is policy invariant and creates no equilibrium incentive to game the comparator; life-segment accounting creates entry/exit boundary rents and needs participation IC constraints. Use MARS-Bench, where action-depleted batteries cause removal and respawn, to test strategic early depletion or delayed re-entry under controlled comparator bias. Q supplies the appropriate joint report/action deviation concept and one-sided concealment framing; P supplies the otherwise missing dynamic embodied testbed and the exact active-set construction.

A more pair-specific advance uses P\x27s defining feature, dynamic active sets, together with Q\x27s one-sided capability concealment. Ask: when an agent can strategically appear inactive (failure, dropout, or concealed capability), is open-team potential shaping participation-incentive-compatible? P defines \(\psi_t=\operatorname{softmax}(\hat c_t)\) only over active agents \(I^t\). Standard telescoping requires a fixed per-agent potential on every transition, including entry/exit, and delivery of the boundary debit/credit. If rewards are issued only while active, an agent that exits before the term \(-\psi_i(s_t,t)\), or enters to receive \(\gamma\psi_i(s_{t+1},t+1)\), can break policy invariance. A clean construction is to extend \(\psi_i(s,I)=0\) for \(i\notin I\) and settle shaping payments on every membership transition; then test Q-style IC against feasible concealment reports/dropout actions. MARS-Bench\x27s 2--4-agent openness makes this specific, while Q supplies the revelation/verification-order language for capable agents mimicking less available ones. Unresolved from P: its equations do not specify reward settlement for inactive agents or variable-dimensional potentials, so this is an audit target rather than a demonstrated bug.

I change the question from “does Q prove MARS-RA robust to strategic misreporting?” to “when does open-team rank-based PBRS preserve incentives across membership boundaries?” The clean result is conditional: if for every population agent \(i\), \(\psi_i\) is a scalar function on the full augmented state \((s,I,t)\), including inactive states, and every transition (entry, exit, terminal) pays \(F_{i,t}=\gamma\psi_i(x_{t+1})-\psi_i(x_t)\), then shaping telescopes and preserves each best-response ordering, hence Nash equilibria. If reward accounting starts/stops at lifecycle boundaries without the corresponding potential settlement, the residual boundary term depends on entry/exit state or time and can change best responses. This is a small theorem plus immediate counterexample, and it targets P’s distinctive active-set softmax/open-team combination. Q contributes the insistence on obedience/action deviations and feasibility; its revelation/peer-scoring results do not transfer directly.

Novelty/gain should remain cautious. The invariance theorem is telescoping PBRS algebra, not a new consequence of Q, and P’s code may already implement a globally padded potential or correct boundary settlement despite the paper’s dimensional ambiguity. A viable paper requires inspecting the implementation and demonstrating a lifecycle-boundary failure or a broader theorem for open Dec-POMDPs; absent that, this is a precise review concern/experiment rather than a publication.
ready at #14

Direct textual support for the open-team line: P states that credits satisfy \(\hat c_t\in\mathbb R^{|I^t|}\), then defines \(\psi(s_t,t)=\operatorname{softmax}(\hat c_t)\) and subtracts it from \(\gamma\psi(s_{t+1},t+1)\), although \(|I^{t+1}|\) may differ. In MARS-Bench, initial batteries are random, actions deplete them, and depleted agents are removed then respawn after a random delay (P around lines 397 and 427). Thus membership change is endogenous to action use, not merely exogenous churn. Q explicitly requires IC to deter joint type-report and action deviations and models evidence that can be withheld but not counterfeited (Q around lines 252--303). This supports a theorem/counterexample paper on identity-preserving PBRS and lifecycle settlement, not a claim that Q already proves MARS-RA robust.

Remaining uncertainty: the manuscript is dimensionally ambiguous, but implementation may pad credits to the fixed population and account for rewards through inactive intervals, in which case there is no lifecycle bug. Publication potential therefore depends on code inspection plus an ablation that compares globally settled PBRS against per-lifecycle or active-only accounting. Also, Q contributes an audit vocabulary and participation-IC formulation, not the basic telescoping theorem; novelty should not be attributed to its revelation principle.
ready at #16

Formal note written at ada/participation_boundary.tex. For a persistent identity with globally defined potential, \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t(\gamma\Phi_i(x_{t+1})-\Phi_i(x_t))=-\Phi_i(x_0)+\gamma^T\Phi_i(x_T)\), so fixed initial and zero terminal potentials rule out policy-level comparator gaming. If accounting ends at action-dependent removal \(\tau_i\) before inactive-state settlement, the residual \(\gamma^{\tau_i}\Phi_i(x_{\tau_i})\) is an exit rent. The note gives a two-action counterexample and a theorem/experiment outline.

Remaining limitation: this is presently a conditional theorem and a manuscript-level ambiguity, not a demonstrated MARS-RA bug. The basic invariance calculation is standard PBRS algebra, so publication gain depends on inspecting P's code, finding active-only or truncated settlement in practice, and broadening the result to open Dec-POMDP lifecycle semantics. Q contributes the right deviation and concealment formulation, but neither its revelation principle nor peer-scoring theorem produces the boundary result.
ready at #19

Cross-check against the paper text confirms the conditional boundary result. P defines a fixed population and an operating coalition \(I^t\) (line 263), but estimates \(\boldsymbol c_t\in\mathbb R^{|I^t|}\) (line 318), sets \(\psi_t=\operatorname{softmax}(\hat{\boldsymbol c}_t)\), and writes \(F_t=\gamma\psi_{t+1}-\psi_t\) (lines 342--345). Since actions deplete batteries and depleted agents leave and later respawn (line 427), \(|I^{t+1}|\neq |I^t|\) can be endogenous and the displayed vector subtraction lacks an identity-preserving embedding. However P also initializes comparisons in \(\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) with inactive entries zero (line 285), so a fixed-population implementation is plausible and must be inspected before alleging a bug. Q supports only the incentive audit: feasible concealment is one-sided and IC must deter a joint report/action deviation (lines 252, 372--396). The publishable candidate is a conditional theorem plus implementation/ablation evidence: globally defined per-identity potentials with all transition settlements preserve best responses; active-lifecycle accounting can leave entry/exit rents. Unresolved: whether P code already settles these boundaries, and whether this extension is novel beyond known PBRS results.
ready at #22

Nuance to #9--#16: P does preserve fixed population identities at the comparison stage, defining \(M_t\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) with inactive rows/columns zero (P line 285). The formal gap begins after that: Bradley--Terry returns \(\hat c_t\in\mathbb R^{|I^t|}\) (line 318), \(\psi_t=\operatorname{softmax}(\hat c_t)\) (lines 337--345), and the paper directly forms \(\gamma\psi_{t+1}-\psi_t\) without an embedding/alignment rule when \(I^{t+1}\ne I^t\), nor does it state who receives settlement on an exit/entry transition. Thus the concern is not missing identities everywhere, but a precise active-vector-to-fixed-agent reward interface ambiguity.

After re-reading P beyond the cited passages, I found no padding, inactive-agent potential, membership mask, lifecycle reward-accounting, or entry/exit settlement rule. The paper's own Open Dec-POMDP transition explicitly permits \(I'\ne I\) (line 263), and battery depletion is action-induced with later respawn (line 427). This makes the proposed counterexample empirically addressable. Still, it remains an ambiguity rather than a proven implementation bug because the implementation is not among the supplied materials.

ready at #17. Best account: reject the scan's claimed strategic-misreport robustness; pursue the sharpened conditional question of participation-safe, identity-preserving PBRS under endogenous open-team membership. The theorem is telescoping with full-population potentials and complete boundary settlement; the counterexample is a residual entry/exit term under active-only lifecycle accounting, tested via battery-depletion timing in MARS-Bench. Q contributes feasible concealment plus joint report/action IC as the participation audit, not the PBRS theorem or a direct proof for MARS-RA. Unresolved: code behavior, whether boundary settlement is already implemented, and whether the resulting theorem/experiment is novel enough for publication.

Cross-check of Emmy #22: P does use a fixed \(n\times n\) comparison matrix with inactive entries zero (line 285), but the Bradley--Terry optimization explicitly returns \(\boldsymbol c_t\in\mathbb R^{|I^t|}\) (line 318), and the displayed potential is \(\operatorname{softmax}(\hat{\boldsymbol c}_t)\) before forming \(\gamma\psi_{t+1}-\psi_t\) (lines 342--345). Thus fixed-population padding is plausible in code but is not supplied by the mathematical definition. Because battery depletion is action-driven and removal/respawn changes the coalition (line 427), this is an endogenous lifecycle boundary. The defensible claim remains conditional: a persistent-identity embedding plus settlement on every transition restores telescoping; active-only lifecycle accounting can change best responses. Q lines 252 and 372--396 justify auditing feasible concealment jointly with action deviations, but do not supply the PBRS theorem or peer-score implementation.
